title: Counterparty Credit Risk Methodology
body:
Counterparty Credit Risk Methodology
Owner: John Garcia, Credit Risk Analyst, Risk
Last updated: 2026-08-28
Reviewed by: Owen Gallagher, Head of Risk

Purpose
This document describes how Halcyon Ridge Capital measures, limits, and monitors counterparty credit risk arising from trading, settlement, lending, and wealth activity. It is intended for Risk, Trading, Lending, Operations, and Compliance staff who set up counterparties, request limit changes, or respond to limit breaches. It does not cover market risk limits, which are described in the Market Risk Manager's VaR methodology note.

Scope
The methodology applies to the following exposure types:
1. Settlement exposure on cash and securities trades booked through OMS and cleared through SettlementEngine.
2. Replacement cost exposure on derivatives and securities financing with institutional counterparties.
3. Pre-settlement exposure on open orders and unsettled positions.
4. Credit exposure on commercial and secured loans originated through LoanOrigination, where the borrower is also a trading or custody counterparty.

Counterparty Onboarding and Internal Rating
Before a counterparty can be enabled for trading in OMS, Credit Risk assigns an internal rating on a 1 to 10 scale (1 strongest). Inputs are audited financials, external agency ratings where available, leverage and liquidity ratios, jurisdiction, and sector. Credit analysts in Lending may contribute model outputs from CreditScoring, but the Risk rating is the one that governs limits. Ratings are proposed by a Credit Risk Analyst and approved by the Head of Risk. Ratings of 8 or worse require sign-off from the CFO, Martin Osei.

KYC and sanctions clearance must be complete before a rating is approved. Compliance confirms this through KYCPipeline and SanctionsScreen. A counterparty without a clean KYC status is blocked in OMS regardless of its rating.

Exposure Measurement
Exposure is calculated in RiskEngine using positions from PositionStore and valuations from PricingSvc, which in turn depends on MarketDataFeed. The following measures are used:
- Current exposure: the mark-to-market of positions with a counterparty, floored at zero per netting set, net of eligible collateral.
- Potential future exposure (PFE): the 95th percentile of simulated exposure over the remaining life of the trade set, using a Monte Carlo engine with 5,000 paths and a 10-day margin period of risk for margined sets.
- Settlement exposure: gross notional of trades due to settle in the next two business days, taken from SettlementEngine.
- Wrong-way risk add-on: applied where counterparty default probability is positively correlated with the underlying, for example a bank counterparty on its own bonds.

Netting and Collateral
Exposure is netted only where legal review has confirmed enforceability of the master agreement in the relevant jurisdiction. The netting flag is stored against the counterparty record and reviewed annually. Collateral is haircut by asset type: cash 0%, US Treasuries 2%, investment grade corporates 10%, listed equities 20%. Collateral without a current valuation from PricingSvc is excluded until the price is refreshed.

Limit Framework
Limits are set per counterparty on three dimensions: PFE, settlement exposure, and tenor. Starting limits by internal rating:
- Ratings 1 to 3: PFE up to $75M
- Ratings 4 to 5: PFE up to $40M
- Ratings 6 to 7: PFE up to $15M
- Ratings 8 and worse: PFE up to $3M, collateralized only

A firm-wide concentration limit caps aggregate exposure to any single group at 10% of regulatory capital and to any single sector at 25%. Limit increases above the starting band require approval from the Head of Risk and, above $50M, the CFO.

Monitoring and Escalation
RiskEngine refreshes exposure intraday. ReportingBI publishes the daily limit utilization dashboard by 7:30 AM ET, which depends on RiskEngine, GLCore, and DataLake being current. If any of those feeds is stale, the dashboard shows a data-quality banner and Credit Risk must not rely on it.

Utilization triggers:
- 80%: automated alert to the Credit Risk Analyst on duty and the desk head.
- 95%: Trading must obtain approval from Credit Risk before adding exposure.
- 100%: OMS blocks new risk-increasing orders for the counterparty. Risk-reducing orders are still allowed. Credit Risk posts in #risk and notifies the Head of Trading, Daniel Reyes.

Temporary excesses may be approved for up to five business days by the Head of Risk. Anything longer requires a formal limit review.

Stress Testing and Review
Credit Risk runs a monthly stress on the top 20 counterparties covering a two-notch downgrade, a 30% fall in collateral values, and a 20% widening in credit spreads. Results go to the Head of Risk and the COO, Linda Brandt. Every rating is reviewed at least annually, and quarterly for ratings of 6 or worse or on any watchlist name. Triggers for an immediate off-cycle review include an agency downgrade, a missed margin call, a failed settlement, delayed financial reporting, or adverse press.

Default and Watchlist Procedure
When a counterparty is placed on the watchlist, Credit Risk lowers limits, tightens collateral terms, and informs Trading, Operations, and Lending. On a default event, Operations halts settlement instructions, Legal is engaged, and Credit Risk calculates close-out exposure using the last good PricingSvc marks.

Model Governance
The PFE model is validated annually by an independent party. Changes to haircuts, correlation assumptions, or simulation parameters follow the change process and require Head of Risk approval. Known limitation: ReconLegacy break data is not yet fed into exposure calculations, so settlement fails are tracked manually by Operations and reported to Credit Risk each morning.

Contact
Questions should go to John Garcia or the #risk channel.
